In 1997, [[Moni Naor]] and [[Omer Reingold]] described efficient constructions for various [[cryptographic primitive]]s in private key as well as [[public-key cryptography]]. Their result is the construction of an efficient [[pseudorandom function family|pseudorandom function]]. Let ''p'' and ''l'' be [[prime number]]s with {{Nowrap|''l'' {{!}} ''p'' &minus; 1}}, and select an element <math> g \in \mathbb{F}_p^*</math> of [[multiplicative order]] ''l''. Then for each (''n''+1)-dimensional [[coordinate vector|vector]] <math> a = (a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathbb{F}_l^{n+1}, </math> they define the function<math display="block">f_{a}(x) = g^{a_0\cdot a_1^{x_1} a_2^{x_2} \cdots a_n^{x_n}} \in \mathbb F_p, </math>where {{Nowrap|1=''x'' = ''x''<sub>1</sub>&mldr;''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is the [[Binary numeral system#Representation|bit representation]] of the integer ''x'', {{Nowrap|0 &le; ''x'' &le; 2<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>}}, with some extra leading zeros if necessary.<ref name="NaorReingold" />

==Example==

Let {{Nowrap|1=''p'' = 7}} and {{Nowrap|1=''l'' = 3}}; then {{Nowrap|''l'' {{!}} ''p'' &minus; 1}}. Select <math>g=4\in\mathbb{F}_7^*</math> of multiplicative order 3 (since {{Nowrap|1=4<sup>3</sup> = 64 &equiv; 1 (mod 7)}}).  For {{Nowrap|1=''n'' = 3}}, {{Nowrap|1=''a'' = (1,1,2,1)}} and {{Nowrap|1=''x'' = 5}} (the bit representation of 5 is 101), we can compute {{Nowrap|''f''<sub>''a''</sub>(5)}} as follows:<math display="block">f_a(5) = 4^{1\cdot 1^1 2^0 1^1} = 4^1 = 4 \in \mathbb{F}_7. </math>

==Efficiency==
The evaluation of function {{Nowrap|''f''<sub>''a''</sub>(5)}} in the Naor–Reingold construction can be done very efficiently: at any given point, it is comparable with one [[modular exponentiation]] and ''n'' modular multiplications. This function can be computed in parallel by threshold circuits of bounded depth and polynomial size.

The Naor–Reingold function can be used as the basis of many [[cryptography|cryptographic]] schemes including [[Symmetric-key algorithm|symmetric encryption]], [[Authentication protocol|authentication]], and [[Digital signature|digital signatures]].

==Security of the function==

Assume that an attacker sees several outputs of the function, such as <math> f_a(1) = g^{a_1},</math> <math> f_a(2) = g^{a_2},</math> <math>f_a(3) = g^{a_1 a_2}, \ldots,</math> <math>f_a(k) = g^{a_1^{x_1} a_2^{x_2}...a_n^{x_n}},</math> and wants to compute <math> f_{a}(k + 1)</math>. Assume for simplicity that <math> x_1=0</math>; then the attacker needs to solve the [[computational Diffie–Hellman assumption|computational Diffie–Hellman (CDH) problem]] between <math> f_a (1)= g^{a_{1}} </math> and <math>f_{a}(k) = g^{a_{2}^{x_{2}} ...a_{n}^{x_{n}}}</math> to get <math>f_{a}(k+1) = g^{a_{1}a_{2}^{x_{2}} \dots a_{n}^{x_{n}}}</math>. In general, moving from <math> k</math> to <math> k+1</math> changes the bit pattern, and unless <math> k+1</math> is a power of 2, one can split the exponent in <math> f_{a}(k + 1)</math> so that the computation corresponds to computing the [[Diffie–Hellman problem|Diffie–Hellman]] key between two of the earlier results. This attacker wants to predict the next sequence element. Such an attack would be very bad—but it is also possible to fight it off by working in [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] with a hard Diffie–Hellman problem (DHP).

=== Example ===
An attacker sees several outputs of the function, such as <math>f_{a}(5) = 4^{1^{1} 2^{0} 1^{1}} = 4^{1} = 4 </math>, as in the previous example, and <math>f_{a}(1) = 4^{1^{0} 2^{0} 1^{1}} = 4^{1} = 4 </math>. Then, the attacker wants to predict the next sequence element of this function, <math> f_{a}(6)</math>. However, the attacker cannot predict the outcome of <math> f_{a}(6) </math> from knowing <math>  f_{a}(1)</math> and <math> f_{a}(5)</math>.

Other attacks could also be very bad for a [[pseudorandom number generator]]: the user expects to get random numbers from the output, so of course the stream should not be predictable, but even more, it should be indistinguishable from a random string. Let <math> \mathcal{A}^f </math> denote the algorithm <math> \mathcal{A} </math> with access to an oracle for evaluating the function <math> f_{a}(x)</math>. Suppose that the [[decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption]] holds for <math> \mathbb F_p </math>; then Naor and Reingold show that for every [[PP (complexity)|probabilistic polynomial time]] algorithm <math> \mathcal{A} </math>  and sufficiently large ''n'',<math display="block"> \text{Pr }[\mathcal{A}^{f_{a}(x)}(p,g) \to 1] - \text{Pr }[\mathcal{A}^{R} (p,g)\to 1] </math>is [[negligible function|negligible]].

The first probability is taken over the choice of the seed <math> s=(p,g,a)</math>, and the second probability is taken over the random distribution induced on <math> p,g</math> by <math> \mathcal{I}\mathcal{G} (n) </math>, instance generator, and the random choice of the function <math> R_{a}(x) </math> among the set of all <math> \{0,1\}^{n} \to \mathbb F_p </math> functions.<ref name="DDHBoneh" />

==Linear complexity==

One natural measure of how useful a sequence may be for [[cryptography|cryptographic]] purposes is the size of its linear complexity. The linear complexity of an ''n''-element sequence <math> W(x)</math> over a ring <math> \mathcal{R}</math> with <math> x=0,1,2,\ldots, n-1</math> is the length <math> l</math> of the shortest linear [[recurrence relation]] <math> W(x+l)=A_{l-1} W(x+l-1) + \cdots A_0 W(x),</math> where <math> x=0,1,2, \ldots, n-l-1</math> with <math> A_0,\ldots,A_{l-1}\in\mathcal{R}</math>, which is satisfied by this sequence.

For some <math> \gamma > 0</math> and <math> n \geq (1+\gamma) \log(l)</math>, for any <math>\delta > 0 </math> and sufficiently large ''l'', the linear complexity of the sequence <math> f_{a}(x)_{x=0}^{2^{n-1}}</math>, denoted by <math>L_a</math> satisfies<math display="block">L_{a} \geqslant \begin{cases}
l^{1-\delta} &\text{if } \gamma \geq 2\\
l^{\left(\tfrac{\gamma}{2-\delta}\right)} &\text{if } \gamma < 2
\end{cases}</math>for all except possibly at most <math>3(l - 1)^{n - \delta}</math> vectors <math>a \in (\mathbb{F}_l)^n</math>.<ref name="ShparlinskiLinearComplexity" />  The bound of this work has disadvantages; namely, it does not apply to the very interesting case <math>\log(p) \approx \log(n) \approx n. </math>

==Uniformity of distribution==

The statistical distribution of <math> f_{a}(x)</math>  is exponentially close to [[Uniform distribution (discrete)|uniform]] for almost all vectors <math>a \in (\mathbb{F}_l)^n</math>.

Let <math>{\mathbf D}_a</math> be the [[Inversive congruential generator|discrepancy]] of the set <math>\{f_a (x)| 0 \leq x \leq 2^{n-1}\}</math>. Thus, if <math>n=\lceil\log(p)\rceil </math> is the bit length of <math>p </math>, then for all vectors <math>a \in (\mathbb{F}_l)^n</math>, the bound <math>{\mathbf D}_a\leq \Delta (l,p)</math> holds, where<math display="block">\Delta (l,p) = \begin{cases}
p^{\left (\tfrac{1-\ \gamma\,\!}{2}\right )}l^{\left (\tfrac{-1}{2}\right )}\log^{2}p &\text{ if } l \geqslant p^{\gamma\,\!}\\
p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{2}\right )}l^{-1}\log^{2}p &\text{ if } p^{\gamma\,\!} > l \geqslant p^{\left (\tfrac{2}{3}\right )}  \\
p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{4}\right )}l^{\left (\tfrac{-5}{8}\right )}\log^{2}p &\text{ if } p^{\left (\tfrac{2}{3}\right )} > l \geqslant p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{2}\right )}  \\
p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{8}\right )}l^{\left (\tfrac{-3}{8}\right )}\log^{2}p &\text{ if } p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{2}\right )} > l \geqslant p^{\left (\tfrac{1}{3}\right )}  \\
\end{cases}</math>and<math display="block">\gamma = 2.5 - \log 3 = 0.9150\ldots.</math>Although this property does not seem to have any immediate cryptographic implications, the inverse fact, namely non-uniform distribution, if true would have disastrous consequences for applications of this function.<ref name="ShparlinskiUniformity" />

==Sequences in elliptic curves==

The [[elliptic curve|elliptic-curve]] version of this function is also of interest. In particular, it may help to improve the cryptographic security of the corresponding system. Let <math>p>3</math> be prime and let <math>E</math> be an elliptic curve; then each vector <math>\mathbf{a}</math> defines a finite sequence in the [[subgroup]] <math>\langle G\rangle</math> as<math display="block">F_{a}(x) = (a_{1}^{x_{1}} a_{2}^{x_{2}}\dots a_{n}^{x_{n}})G, </math>where <math>x = x_1 \cdots  x_n</math>  is the bit representation of integer <math>x, 0 \leq x \leq 2^{n-1}</math>. The Naor–Reingold elliptic curve sequence is defined as<ref name="EllipticNaor" /><math display="block"> u_{k} = X (f_{a}(k)), </math>where <math>X(P)</math> is the [[Abscissa and ordinate|abscissa]] of <math>P \in E(\mathbb{F}_p)</math>.

If the [[decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption]] holds, then index <math> k </math> is not enough to compute <math>u_k</math> in polynomial time, even if an attacker performs polynomially-many queries to a [[random oracle]].
